---
title: "Social science data sources"
subtitle: "Foundation to intermediate – where data are held, and the routes to the data of the case study"
---



Where the data analysed by social scientists are held, and how a researcher obtains them, are the two questions addressed in this module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd). The Europeanisation and the economy case study takes its Eurobarometer waves from the GESIS archive, under an account and terms of use that forbid passing the waves on, and the economic series of its panel from the World Bank and Eurostat. The records of the checks made on the claim by SCORE and by the SCORE robustness study (Aczel et al. 2026) are held on the Open Science Framework (OSF), while the other side of the exchange, the deposit of a finished piece of work in a place where others can find it, is covered by the [repositories module](repositories.qmd).

Two matters fall outside the scope of this page. Qualitative data archives are not discussed, although both the UK Data Service, which appears in the tables below, and the Qualitative Data Repository hold qualitative collections. Nor does anything presented here replace the terms of use of a particular dataset, which change, and which you read before you download.

## 1. Three ways in {#sec-access}

Almost every dataset listed on this page is reached by one of three routes, and the vocabulary used by the archives follows the same division.

**Open download.** The file is held on a public page or behind a public API (an interface through which a program, rather than a person at a browser, asks a server for data), under a licence that permits reuse with attribution, typically Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY), a dedication to the public domain such as CC0, or an open government licence. World Bank indicators, the aggregate tables published by Eurostat, the public-use files of the US statistical agencies and most replication packages in political science belong to this kind. Nothing is asked of you beyond the citation and, in the case of official surveys, respect for the rules that protect the respondents.

**Registration and licence.** You create an account under your own name, agree to a set of conditions (no redistribution, no attempt to identify anyone, citation of the source, sometimes non-commercial use) and download the file. This is the standard route for survey microdata, meaning files with one row per respondent: the European Social Survey, the Eurobarometer at GESIS, the safeguarded collection of the UK Data Service, SHARE, IPUMS. Registration is free and immediate, or nearly so, and the archive keeps a record of who downloaded what.

**Application and secure access.** Here the data are too detailed to leave the archive, as with linked administrative records, fine geography, exact dates of birth or business microdata. You apply with a project description, your institution may have to be recognised as a research entity, you may have to complete a training course and become an accredited researcher, and you then work either on a scientific-use file sent under contract or inside a secure environment where nothing leaves without being checked. Examples include the microdata held by Eurostat, the controlled collection of the UK Data Service through SecureLab, the Secure Research Service of the Office for National Statistics and the contract route of the German Socio-Economic Panel, and for any of these routes you should allow weeks or months.

Two distinctions apply across all three routes. **Microdata against aggregates:** a respondent-level file requires the second or third route, while the country-year or region-year tables computed from it are usually open, and the country-year panel used in the workshop is an aggregate of this kind, open but built from licensed microdata. **Catalogue against archive:** a catalogue such as the CESSDA Data Catalogue or re3data indicates that a dataset exists and where it is held, while registration and download take place at the archive that holds it.

The Europeanisation case study takes the second route, its data, sixteen waves of the Standard Eurobarometer, being held by GESIS and downloaded by hand after registration. As the terms of use forbid passing the files on, the workshop distributes country-year aggregates only, under CC BY 4.0.

## 2. The map {#sec-map}

Each of the tables below names the source, what it holds, how it is reached and where to start. In the column on access, 'Open' corresponds to the first route above, 'registration' to the second and 'application' to the third, with a note on what the registration or application involves wherever that is not obvious. The tables are intended as a starting point for a question of your own rather than as a census of the field.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Pick a question you have worked on, or would like to. Find a dataset that could answer it in two of the catalogues above, the CESSDA Data Catalogue and re3data, and write down for each: the archive that holds it, the access route, and the first step you would have to take on Monday morning. If the two catalogues disagree about where the data are, note the disagreement as well.
:::

## 3. The routes of the case study {#sec-course}

The subsections below proceed from the most restricted source to the most open: the GESIS archive, which holds the Eurobarometer waves, then the World Bank and Eurostat, from which the panel takes its country-level series, and finally the OSF, which holds the files of SCORE and its robustness study. Each route is written as a sequence of steps that you can follow from a fresh R session. Code that downloads a file is shown but not run on this page, which is built without a connection, and the results printed beside such code come from the copies kept by the workshop. None of these steps is needed for the tasks of the exercise, whose data are already in place.

Every download described in this section ends with a check that the file is the one used by the workshop. The simplest check is a checksum such as the MD5 sum, a short code that is computed from the contents of a file and changes whenever a single byte of that file changes, and two files with the same MD5 sum are therefore the same file. In R the sum is computed by `tools::md5sum()`, and several of the sources publish it beside the file.

### 3.1 The GESIS archive: the Eurobarometer waves {#sec-gesis}

The outcomes of the Europeanisation case study are built from sixteen Eurobarometer waves fielded between 2004 and 2013, the waves that included the question asking what the European Union means to the respondent personally, with its fourteen items. The files are distributed by **GESIS – Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences**, the German social-science archive, which describes itself as "[the largest German infrastructure institute for the social sciences](https://www.gesis.org/en/institute)" and which runs the Eurobarometer Data Service for the European Commission. In the words of the service, "Eurobarometer data and documentation can be downloaded free of charge from the GESIS Data Catalog", and "the data are available to the scientific community for research and education" ([Eurobarometer Data Service](https://www.gesis.org/en/eurobarometer-data-service)). Every step below was checked in a browser on 8 September 2026, and the file obtained from GESIS at the end proved byte for byte identical to the one from which the country-year panel was built.

The sixteen studies are listed in the table below. Each of them belongs to the access category labelled by GESIS "0 – Data and documents are released for everybody", for which a free account is all that is needed. GESIS re-releases files under new version numbers; the build script checks what you downloaded against this list.

The steps below are clicked rather than scripted, since the route is manual, with registration through a web form with a captcha, a purpose of use requested in your own name at every download, and no maintained R package to script the clicks (the one CRAN package that did so, gesisdata, has not been updated since 2023).

**Before you start: two settings in the browser.** As GESIS serves its pages in German by default while marking them as English, Chrome quietly translates the pages into an English that differs slightly from the English version of the site, and the labels on your screen will not match the ones below. Turn translation off for the site (the translate icon in the address bar, then "Never translate this site") and click **English** in the page header. The sidebar then reads *Datasets / Questionnaires / Codebook* rather than *Datensätze / Fragebögen*.

![The catalogue as it first appears in a browser set to English: German, with the language switch at the top right.](../assets/gesis/00-german-default.jpg){.border}

**1. Register once, before the workshop.** Open [search.gesis.org](https://search.gesis.org/), click *Login* and then "You are not yet registered?". The form asks for your name, country, discipline, email and a password of at least eight characters with a capital letter, a number and a special character. GESIS offers a single kind of account and makes no institutional check, the registration page stating that "Registration at GESIS is free of charge, open to all". As the registration form carries a captcha and cannot be scripted, it should be completed in the week before the workshop. One trap lies in the checkbox that says "I have read the GESIS Usage Regulations", which links to the data-protection notice rather than to the terms of use, found at [gesis.org/en/institute/data-usage-terms](https://www.gesis.org/en/institute/data-usage-terms) and summarised below.

![The registration form, upper half.](../assets/gesis/08-register-top.jpg){.border}

![The registration form, lower half, with the password rule and the two checkboxes.](../assets/gesis/09-register-bottom.jpg){.border}

**2. Find each study by its number.** Type the study number, `ZA4056`, into the search box and press Enter, and the search returns one hit. Do not search by wave name. A search for "Eurobarometer 61.0" returns about nine hundred datasets, with the 2023–2026 waves at the top and the one you want nowhere on the first page, while a `?q=` address pasted into the browser fills the box without running the search. The direct address `https://search.gesis.org/research_data/ZA4056` also works, and the table above links every study in this way.

![Searching by wave name: nine hundred hits, the wanted study not among them.](../assets/gesis/01-search-wave-number.jpg){.border}

![Searching by study number: one hit.](../assets/gesis/02-search-za-number.jpg){.border}

**3. Read the study page.** The page gives the title, the version, the DOI, the fieldwork dates and the countries, and, in the right-hand panel, three download links: *Datasets*, *Questionnaires* and *Codebook*. The questionnaires and the codebook, which download without an account, are the documents that state which variable records which question in that wave, and the [data management module](data-management.qmd#sec-europeanisation) draws on these documents.

![The study page of ZA4056, with the Downloads panel on the right.](../assets/gesis/03-study-page.jpg){.border}

**4. Download the Stata file.** Click *Datasets*. A dialog lists four files: an SPSS portable file, a syntax file defining missing values, the Stata file and the SPSS file. Take the Stata file only, the one ending in `.dta`. The workshop's script reads that format with its labels, and the other three files are not needed. Above the list is a **Purpose of use** dropdown, in which you state a purpose in your own name. Choose "in the course of my studies" if you are a student, and "for further education and qualification" otherwise. The option "in a course as lecturer" is for the lecturer and not for participants. Signed out, the same click produces only a "Login required" box. Signed in, the file arrives under the name given in the table, with no further prompt.

![The download dialog, signed in, with the purpose-of-use dropdown and the four files.](../assets/gesis/04-download-datasets.jpg){.border}

![The same click when signed out.](../assets/gesis/07-login-required.jpg){.border}

**5. Put all sixteen in one folder** outside the workspace, and run the build script described in the [data management module](data-management.qmd#sec-europeanisation). The script unpacks the two zipped studies, reads the sixteen files, checks each against the checksum of the file from which the workshop was built, and writes a single respondent-level file into a folder that the workspace never commits.

**The terms you accepted.** The terms of use, valid since 4 February 2026, are the document linked from every download dialog, and four of the clauses in that document govern how the workshop handles these files. Redistribution: "The provision of the database to third parties is not permitted", and third parties "include, but are not limited to, publishers, libraries, data archives, or research data repositories", which is why no respondent-level file is placed in any repository, public or private. Identification: "The presentation or publication of individual cases, even if there is no direct reference to individuals, is not permitted", while "summary presentations of data, as is customary in scientific papers and lectures, are permitted", and this is the line separating the microdata from the aggregates distributed with this workshop. Citation: the DOI and the version number of each file must appear in anything published from the files. The fourth clause, which bears on any course taught with AI assistants, reads "The use of AI systems for processing the database provided to the user by GESIS is prohibited", with exceptions only on request. In practice, the clause means that the respondent file is never opened in a session that an AI assistant can read, never pasted into a chat, and never handed to an assistant with access to the objects in your R session. The aggregates distributed with the workshop are not covered by this restriction. The terms also ask for the files to be deleted at the end of the project, and set a contractual penalty of €10,000 for a breach of the clauses on redistribution and de-anonymisation.

![The access categories, from the terms of use: the sixteen Eurobarometer studies are all in the first row.](../assets/gesis/06-access-categories.jpg){.border}

The terms permit the sharing of aggregates coarse enough that no respondent can be recovered, and such aggregates, released under a licence of their own, are all that this workshop shares from the Eurobarometer. The licence section of the [data codebook](../data/europeanisation_cy_codebook.md) records this division, with CC BY 4.0 applying to the derived country-year panel and the GESIS terms to everything beneath it. The rebuild for this workshop started from these sixteen files and averaged the respondents 'as interviewed', one of the two options offered by the decision [Cell weighting](../menu.qmd#cell-weighting) in the specification menu, where the alternative is explained.

### 3.2 The macro indicators, at the World Bank {#sec-worldbank}

Two of the country-level series in the country-year panel are taken from the World Development Indicators, published by the World Bank under its open licence (CC BY 4.0):

- `unemp`: unemployment as a percentage of the total labour force, the national estimate, indicator `SL.UEM.TOTL.NE.ZS`, which the Bank republishes from ILOSTAT;
- `growth`: annual GDP growth in percent, indicator `NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG`.

A series can be obtained in two ways. On the site, open [data.worldbank.org](https://data.worldbank.org/), search the indicator code, choose the countries and years and download a CSV. In R, the `WDI` package (version 2.8.0 on CRAN, released in August 2026) performs the same steps in a single call, returning a tidy country-year table:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
macro <- WDI::WDI(
  country   = c("AT", "BE", "BG", "CY", "CZ", "DE", "DK", "EE", "ES", "FI", "FR", "GB",
                "GR", "HU", "IE", "IT", "LT", "LU", "LV", "MT", "NL", "PL", "PT", "RO",
                "SE", "SI", "SK"),
  indicator = c(unemp = "SL.UEM.TOTL.NE.ZS", growth = "NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG"),
  start = 2004, end = 2013
)
```
:::


Other estimates of the same quantity are also published by the Bank, among them the ILO modelled estimate, while Eurostat publishes series of its own, built from the EU Labour Force Survey and fetched from the Eurostat database. The series used in the Europeanisation case study besides the two above, and the reasons why two of these series are not on the curve of the claim, are presented in the next section.

The third macro variable in the country-year panel, `bailout`, is not downloaded at all, being coded instead from the record of EU and IMF financial assistance programmes, country by country and year by year, with the programmes and years used listed in the codebook. Many contextual variables enter a panel in this way, through a documented rule applied by hand and with the source of each fact stated.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Run the `WDI` call above in your workspace and compare its `unemp` column with the one in `europeanisation_cy.csv` for one country. They should agree to the decimal for most country-years and differ for a few, because the Bank revises series after the fact. Write down which years differ and by how much. Any macro series can change between downloads in this way, which is why the codebook records the download date.

### 3.3 The published series {#sec-series}

For each of the two economic measures, the specification menu of the Europeanisation case study offers more than one published series, and the choice among these series is a measurement decision, because the series measure one construct, the national unemployment rate or the growth of output, in slightly different ways. For unemployment the menu offers five series: the national estimate of the World Bank described above (`wb_nat`), which is the series used in the country-year panel and by the reanalyst C6HJR, and four series cut from the Eurostat tables merged by the other reanalysts. These four comprise the rate in the labour force aged 15–74 from the table `une_rt_a_h` (`es_1574_act`, the series used by 018OL), the unemployed as a share of the whole population aged 20–64 from the same table (`es_2064_pop`, KQXUE), the rate in the labour force aged 25–64 from the Labour Force Survey table `lfsa_urgan` (`es_2564_lfs`, the annual counterpart of the quarterly series used by PRL47), and the rate in the labour force aged 15–74 from the short table `tipsun20` (`es_1574_tips`, KEVF1). For growth the menu offers two, the World Bank series and the national accounts published by Eurostat in the table `nama_10_gdp` (`es_growth`). All seven series are stored for the 270 country-years in `data/macro/predictor_measures.csv`, allowing the workspace to merge them without a connection, while the Eurostat tables are kept in the source repository as they were retrieved.

The four unemployment series that cover all 270 country-years differ in age band and denominator, and the population-based series used by KQXUE is a different quantity from a labour-force rate, yet within countries the four series move together. Once the mean of each country and of each year has been removed, the series correlate with one another at between 0.995 and 0.999, and all four therefore remain on the curve, where the choice among them accounts for 0.1% of the variance in the claim-aligned partial correlations.

The other two series were excluded from the curve, because choosing either of them changes who is in the analysis as well as how the economy is measured. The table `tipsun20` has rows for 139 of the 270 country-years, in 26 countries, with none for the United Kingdom and, before 2009, rows for only France and Sweden. Choosing this series therefore halves the panel and shifts the question towards the crisis years. Swapped into the 768 unemployment specifications of the curve, the series leaves 87.0% of them below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, against 82.7% of the unemployment specifications on the curve itself, and changes the class of 18.9% of the pairs. Its choice amounts to a decision about the sample presented as one about the measure, which is why the [decision map](../menu.qmd#map) rewrites the population in the estimand statement whenever the series is chosen. The Eurostat growth series, with no row for the United Kingdom and 260 country-years in 26 countries, costs one country for the same reason, although within the countries that it covers it moves with the World Bank series and leaves the class of every one of its 96 pairs unchanged. Coverage of this kind deserves to be checked before any series is merged, since a merge that silently drops rows alters the population of the question without altering a line of the model.

### 3.4 The OSF: the files of SCORE {#sec-osf}

The Open Science Framework holds both the dossier kept by SCORE on the paper and the components in which the analysts taking part in the robustness study deposited their materials, and the [repositories module](repositories.qmd#sec-score-dossiers) reads that dossier as a record. A public file on the OSF needs no account, every file having a short address of five characters, and `https://osf.io/download/` followed by that address returning the file itself. The `osfr` package (version 0.2.9 on CRAN, released in September 2022, with development continuing on GitHub under rOpenSci) reaches the same files through the OSF API and lists the contents of a project or a component. The case study takes a single file from the OSF, the country-year panel, `europeanisation_cy.csv`, held in the main folder of [osf.io/6zqct](https://osf.io/6zqct/), the fork, maintained by the facilitator, of the record kept by the robustness study for analyst C6HJR. The workspace script `R/get_data.R` fetches this file with osfr as an exercise, falling back on the committed copy when the network or the OSF is unavailable.

As a checksum is computed from the bytes of a file, a program that rewrites the line endings of a text file changes the checksum without changing a single value. Git on Windows does this to CSV files unless it is told otherwise, which is why a value-by-value comparison, as in the [data management module](data-management.qmd#sec-reproduce), is the safer check of a text file that has passed through a repository.

As every OSF project becomes read-only from 19 February 2027, these files will still download at the same addresses while the maintained copy of the country-year panel moves to the [`ar4ds-eu-workspace`](https://github.com/CodeMoreh/ar4ds-eu-workspace) repository on GitHub. The implications of the change for depositing your own work are discussed in the [repositories module](repositories.qmd#sec-osf).

## 4. Citing data {#sec-citing}

A dataset is cited in the same way as a publication, with the producer, the title, the version or wave, the distributor and the persistent identifier, and most archives print the citation that they expect on the study page. The archives listed in the map ask for the citation in different forms:

- **The Harvard Dataverse** prints a citation for every dataset, with its version and a **UNF**, a checksum computed by Dataverse from the values in the data rather than from the bytes of the file, so that the same data saved in another format yield the same UNF.
- **The ESS** provides a citation for each data file, with its edition and DOI, and asks that a modified file be cited as "Adapted from ESS Round X, version number X".
- **NCHS** assigns no DOI to the NSFG files, and a citation therefore names the agency, the survey, the cycle and the file, with the date of download.
- **GESIS** asks for the study number, the DOI and the version of each wave, which are given for the sixteen waves of the Europeanisation case study in the table of section 3.1.
- **The World Bank** asks for the indicator and the date of access.

Two further habits make it easier for a reader to repeat your analysis. Record the date on which you downloaded a series, because the World Bank and Eurostat revise past years without renaming the file, and a reader who repeats your download a year later will obtain slightly different numbers. And keep the version identifier of a survey file, because the ESS, SHARE, the NSFG and the Eurobarometer all release corrected editions of the same round.
